page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: Sources > Blood flow in skin (Häfner et al., 2008 annotation) - the sentence carrying claim D001
sentence_as_it_stands: The one ropivacaine flow recording past 90 minutes: [dose figure omitted] at the base of the finger raised fingertip flow by 155.2 percent, still raised at 24 hours, in 20 volunteers. Limits: a finger block with flow read at the fingertip, not a wheal with flow read at the injection site.
quote: After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes. … 24 hours after injection the acral perfusion reduced to +35.1% (p = 0.03) in comparison to the initial perfusion values before injection (Table 2).
corrected_wording: One of two ropivacaine flow recordings past 90 minutes, both from the same Tübingen department and both after a finger block rather than at a wheal: at the base of the finger it raised fingertip flow by 155.2 percent, still raised at 24 hours, in 20 volunteers. The companion study recorded finger skin perfusion by laser Doppler at 12 points out to 24 hours after a plain-ropivacaine digital nerve block in 20 volunteers, 20 fingers per arm, and found flow still significantly above baseline at 24 hours (Schnabl 2013, PMID 23076005). Limits on both: a finger block with flow read away from the injection site, not a wheal with flow read at the injection site.
notes: The annotation's own figures for Häfner 2008 all check out against that paper's abstract (+155.2%, sustained vasodilatation still demonstrable at 24 h, 20 test persons, Oberst's-method block), and its 'Limits' line is right. Only the word 'one' fails. Schnabl 2013 is absent from this page entirely - a text search of the fetched page for 'Schnabl' returns nothing - although the Ropivacaine Wheals page has carried it since at least 2026-10-02 and has already recorded there that the 'nobody past 90 minutes' claim is wrong as stated. The two pages are out of step.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each drug do to blood vessels in skin? (final paragraph); and What would settle what is unresolved ('What happens to skin blood flow at a wheal after the first ninety minutes?') - claim D000
sentence_as_it_stands: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a wheal of any of these drugs for longer than ninety minutes. The longer recordings were made elsewhere: ropivacaine at the fingertip for 24 hours after a block at the base of the finger, where it raised flow and kept it raised (Häfner et al., 2008), and lidocaine and bupivacaine under the skin for 6 hours, where flow was back to baseline by 30 minutes (Liu et al., 1995).
quote: A two-injection dorsal technique digital nerve block for local anesthesia of the finger nerve bundles (Oberst's-method anaesthetic block) was performed on index and ring finger of both hands in each volunteer at the base of the fingers. … After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes.
corrected_wording: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a wheal of any of these drugs for longer than ninety minutes. The longer recordings were made elsewhere: ropivacaine in the finger for 24 hours after a block at the base of the finger, in two studies from the same department, where it raised flow and kept it raised (Häfner 2008, PMID 18334782, read at the fingertip; Schnabl 2013, PMID 23076005, read on the back of the finger below the nail), and lidocaine and bupivacaine under the skin for 6 hours, where flow was back to baseline by 30 minutes (Liu et al., 1995).
notes: The leading sentence is correct and the paper does not disturb it - a digital nerve block is not a wheal, and the flow probe sat remote from the injection. Only the list of longer recordings is incomplete. Low rather than medium because nothing downstream turns on the count.

section: PART II - HOW LONG IT LASTS > 5.5 The rest of the duration literature, and what each figure is measuring (Schnabl entry); and PART XI > 14. The rejected-claims table, row 'Schnabl's recording ran to 60 minutes'
sentence_as_it_stands: The original paper could not be obtained from the publisher, so the exact timepoint list is secondary-source verified rather than primary-methods verified. State it as "beyond 60 minutes, apparently 24 hours.
quote: After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes. … 24 hours after injection the acral perfusion reduced to +35.1% (p = 0.03) in comparison to the initial perfusion values before injection (Table 2).
corrected_wording: The recording schedule is now read from the paper's own methods rather than inferred: perfusion was recorded at 12 points spanning 1440 minutes - before injection, then 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360 and 1440 minutes - and Tables 2 to 5 report all 12 points, so every arm including plain ropivacaine was followed to 24 hours. Plain ropivacaine peaked at +160.2% at 56 minutes, was +129.7% at 6 hours and was still significantly above baseline at 24 hours (+35.1%, p = 0.03). Pain was tested separately at 0, 16, 32, 48, 60, 360 and 1400 minutes. The entry can move from ABSTRACT-ONLY to FULLTEXT.
notes: This is the paper's own open question and the page's own acknowledged soft spot: the page says the timepoint list is secondary-source verified and tells the reader to state a hedged form. The full text is in the project packet at helper-S1/texts/S-686-28.txt (14 pages), so it is now obtainable. One caveat to carry: the 1440-minute row of Table 2 repeats the 24-minute row's mean and SD (47.9 PU, SD 30.2), so the body text's +35.1% is the reliable figure at that timepoint, not the table's mean.

section: PART XII - SOURCES > 15.1 Vessels in skin - the core (Schnabl register entry)
sentence_as_it_stands: Schnabl SM, Herrmann N, Wilder D, Breuninger H, Häfner HM. Skin perfusion and pain evaluation with different local anaesthetics in a double blind randomized study following digital nerve block anaesthesia. Clinical Hemorheology and Microcirculation 2013;55(2):241-253. DOI 10.3233/CH-2012-1629.
quote: Saskia M. Schnabla , Frank Unglaubb , Zarqa Leitzc , Helmut Breuningera
corrected_wording: Schnabl SM, Unglaub F, Leitz Z, Breuninger H, Häfner HM. Skin perfusion and pain evaluation with different local anaesthetics in a double blind randomized study following digital nerve block anaesthesia. Clinical Hemorheology and Microcirculation 2013;55(2):241-253. PMID 23076005. DOI 10.3233/CH-2012-1629.
notes: Two of the five authors are wrong: 'Herrmann N, Wilder D' should be 'Unglaub F, Leitz Z'. The title page gives Saskia M. Schnabl, Frank Unglaub, Zarqa Leitz, Helmut Breuninger and Hans-Martin Häfner, and Europe PMC's record for PMID 23076005 gives the same five. The page is internally inconsistent: section 5.5 cites it correctly as 'Schnabl, Unglaub, Leitz et al. 2013'. Also worth adding: the `UNSOURCED` note in this same entry ('The "60-minute recording limit" attributed to this paper in earlier project notes is not in the abstract and is probably wrong') is now settled - it is wrong, and the real schedule runs to 1440 minutes.

section: PART I > 4.11 What remains unmeasured about vessels, item 2 ('Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes'); and PART XI > 14. The rejected-claims table, row 'Nobody has recorded ropivacaine skin flux past 90 minutes'
sentence_as_it_stands: Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes. Cederholm's recordings stop there. The nearest thing is Häfner 2008, which followed [dose figure omitted] ropivacaine flux for 24 hours - but at a fingerpad after an Oberst block, where the injection is at the digit base and the measurement at the pad, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site.
quote: A two-injection dorsal technique digital nerve block for local anesthesia of the finger nerve bundles (Oberst's-method anaesthetic block) was performed on index and ring finger of both hands in each volunteer at the base of the fingers. … After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes.
corrected_wording: Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes. Cederholm's recordings stop there. There are two nearest things, not one, both from the same department and both after an Oberst block rather than at a wheal: Häfner 2008 (PMID 18334782) followed flux at the fingerpad for 24 hours, and Schnabl 2013 (PMID 23076005) followed it on the back of the finger below the nail at 12 points out to 24 hours. In both the injection is at the digit base and the measurement away from it, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site, and neither is a wheal.
notes: The gap itself is unchanged and the section's own conclusion - narrow the claim to 'at a wheal' - is correct. Only the count of near misses is short, and Schnabl is the one of the two whose schedule is now primary-verified.

section: PART VII - THE 0.25% DECISION > 10.1 Two premises in the question are false > False premise 1
sentence_as_it_stands: The only preparation where [dose figure omitted] raises perfusion is the finger after a digital block: Schnabl 2013 at +160.2% and Häfner 2008 at +155.2% sustained to 24 h. Drug deposited around named nerves at the digit base, measured at the pad, injection trauma not at the measurement site. That is not a wheal.
quote: To quantify changes in skin perfusion, in every group acral skin blood flux was measured via laser doppler flowmetry (LDF, Perimed Master 4001 and Perimed PF2b, Sweden; wave length 780 nm) on the dorsal side of the fingers below the nail bed.
corrected_wording: The only preparation where it raises perfusion is the finger after a digital block: Schnabl 2013 at +160.2%, still significantly raised at 24 h, and Häfner 2008 at +155.2% sustained to 24 h. Drug deposited around named nerves at the digit base; measured on the back of the finger below the nail in Schnabl and at the fingerpad in Häfner; injection trauma not at the measurement site in either. That is not a wheal.
notes: 'measured at the pad' is true of Häfner 2008, which read flux at the fingerpads of D II and D IV, but not of Schnabl 2013, which measured on the dorsal side of the fingers below the nail bed. Schnabl tested pain on the pulp, which may be where the conflation comes from. The argument this passage makes is unaffected - a site on the back of the finger is still remote from an injection at the digit base - so the conclusion stands and only the design detail needs fixing. Schnabl's own 24-hour figure (+35.1%, p = 0.03) could also be added, since the sentence currently attaches 'sustained to 24 h' only to Häfner.

page: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a local anaesthetic wheal beyond 90 minutes, so late pallor after an injection falls outside every published measurement window
section: Evidence / Receipt property, 'WHAT CAME BACK, all of it short of the mark' (first item)
sentence_as_it_stands: Cederholm 1991, the only human intradermal ropivacaine series, stops at 90 minutes and says so.
quote: Skin blood flow after intradermal injection of ropivacaine in various concentrations with and without epinephrine evaluated by laser Doppler flowmetry, Reg Anesth 17 (1992)
corrected_wording: Two human intradermal ropivacaine laser Doppler series exist and both stop at 90 minutes: Cederholm 1991 (PMID 2038927), a methodological study whose Group III injected ropivacaine intradermally in 12 people, and Cederholm 1992 (PMID 1286053), the dedicated study of skin blood flow after intradermal ropivacaine at several concentrations with and without epinephrine in 23 volunteers. A third intradermal ropivacaine study, Cederholm 1994 (PMID 8067217), scored vessels by visual inspection rather than measuring flow.
notes: The absence this record asserts is unaffected and if anything better supported, because the second series also stops at 90 minutes - Europe PMC's abstract for PMID 1286053 states 'Recordings were made at 20, 40, 60, and 90 minutes after intradermal injection'. But 'the only' is wrong, and the two papers are not interchangeable: the 1992 one is the study the other pages lean on, and the Ropivacaine Wheals page treats it separately in its gap 6 and in section 4.3. S-686-28 carries the 1992 paper as reference [3].

page: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a local anaesthetic wheal beyond 90 minutes, so late pallor after an injection falls outside every published measurement window
section: Evidence / Receipt property, 'WHAT CAME BACK, all of it short of the mark' (Haefner item); Status property
sentence_as_it_stands: Haefner 2008 recorded 24 hours of flux after ropivacaine [dose figure omitted], but at a fingerpad after an Oberst block at the digit base, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site, which is why its saline arm showed no change at all.
quote: After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes.
corrected_wording: Haefner 2008 (PMID 18334782) recorded 24 hours of flux after ropivacaine, but at a fingerpad after an Oberst block at the digit base, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site, which is why its saline arm showed no change at all. Schnabl 2013 (PMID 23076005) is a second recording of the same kind from the same department, read on the back of the finger below the nail at 12 points out to 1440 minutes after a digital nerve block, with plain ropivacaine still significantly above baseline at 24 hours. Both are blocks rather than wheals, so neither closes this absence.
notes: The finding this record asserts still stands, and it is the canonical receipt for the claim, so the near-miss list should be complete. Schnabl 2013 is the nearest miss of all of them - ropivacaine, 24 hours, randomised and double-blind - and is the only one whose recording schedule is now verified from the primary methods. Separately, this record's Status is Open and its verification state unverified: an independent re-check through Europe PMC (ropivacaine AND intradermal AND skin blood flow / laser Doppler, 12 hits) returned nothing at a wheal beyond 90 minutes, so the absence can be recorded as re-confirmed, with the caveat that the engine was Europe PMC and not PubMed, which was unreachable in this session.

section: Literature - ropivacaine's intrinsic cutaneous vasoconstriction > What the cited studies establish about duration
sentence_as_it_stands: No cited study measured skin blood flow beyond 90 minutes. The three primary studies stop at 30 minutes, 90 minutes, and an unreported endpoint, respectively. The evidence therefore cannot determine whether ropivacaine's effect on skin blood flow lasts two, four, or six hours.
quote: skin perfusion values reached +160.2% (p = 0.008) after 56 minutes and +129.7% (p = 0.01) after 6 hours. … 24 hours after injection the acral perfusion reduced to +35.1% (p = 0.03) in comparison to the initial perfusion values before injection (Table 2).
corrected_wording: No study cited on this page measured skin blood flow beyond 90 minutes: the three primary studies stop at 30 minutes, 90 minutes and an unreported endpoint. Those studies cannot determine whether ropivacaine's effect on skin blood flow lasts two, four or six hours. Evidence beyond 90 minutes does exist by a different route: after a plain-ropivacaine digital nerve block, finger skin perfusion was still raised at 6 hours and at 24 hours in two randomised double-blind volunteer studies (Häfner 2008, PMID 18334782; Schnabl 2013, PMID 23076005). Those are nerve blocks with the probe away from the injection site, not intradermal or subcutaneous wheals, so they do not settle the question for this page's route.
notes: The first two sentences are correctly scoped to the page's own citations. The third generalises to 'the evidence' and is too broad: the question it calls undecidable has an answer by the digital-block route, and the answer runs the opposite way to this section's heading - plain ropivacaine at the strength used was vasodilatative for 6 hours and still measurably raised at 24. The route caveat must travel with any correction, which is why this is a scope fix rather than a reversal of the section.
